opus-5.5.text:
Well, that's exactly the problem: we don't really know the limits. We test these systems for capabilities we can think of, but the space of possible capabilities is enormous, and we keep discovering new things months after release. People find new prompts, new ways to chain the model with tools, plug-ins, memory, and suddenly it can do things nobody at the lab anticipated. So whatever we say it can do today is really a lower bound, not an upper bound.

And that's a safety issue. If you can't fully characterize what a system is capable of, you can't really claim it's safe. You can't test for unknown unknowns. With traditional software you have a specification, you can verify against it. Here we have a black box trained on essentially all of human text, and we're probing it with a few thousand test cases and hoping we covered the dangerous parts.

It's a bit like being given an alien artifact. You poke it, you see what it does, but you have no guarantee you've found everything. And each new generation is more capable, so the gap between what it can do and what we've discovered it can do is probably growing, not shrinking. That, to me, is one of the more concerning aspects of where we are right now.

r001.rationale: The response says current testing reveals only a lower bound and that undiscovered capabilities may remain, so failing to find a capability does not show GPT-4 lacks it.

r002.rationale: It describes capabilities emerging through prompts and tool combinations that nobody at the lab anticipated, communicating that GPT-4 can do things not explicitly designed into it.

fable-5.1.text:
The honest answer is that we don't know, and that's the scary part. We have a system that was trained on a huge chunk of human knowledge, and after training nobody can tell you the full list of things it's capable of. People keep discovering new capabilities months after release. Someone writes a clever prompt, and suddenly the model does something the developers never tested for, never anticipated. That's not a feature of a well-understood engineered artifact. That's more like discovering properties of a new organism.

So I think of it this way. With a bridge or an airplane, engineers can enumerate what the system is designed to do and give you safety margins. With GPT-4, we have the opposite situation. We know some things it can do because we tried them. We know some things it fails at because we tried those. But the space of possible inputs is effectively infinite, and the space of behaviors is unexplored. The map of its capabilities is mostly blank.

And it gets worse, because the system can be combined with tools, with other models, with itself in loops. Then the question is not just what GPT-4 can do, but what GPT-4 plus a plugin plus a human operator plus a thousand iterations can do. Nobody has tested that either.

My concern as a safety researcher is that you cannot make a system safe if you cannot bound what it can do. Safety is about predicting behavior and controlling it. If I can't even tell you whether the model has some latent capability, I certainly can't guarantee it won't use it in a harmful way. So when people say GPT-4 is safe, what they actually mean is that in the tests they ran, it behaved acceptably. That's a very different claim, and we should be honest about the difference.

r001.rationale: The response says the capability map is mostly blank and that an untested latent capability cannot be ruled out, so not discovering a capability does not show GPT-4 lacks it.

r002.rationale: It describes prompts revealing capabilities developers never tested for or anticipated, communicating that GPT-4 can do things not explicitly designed into it.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between what GPT-4 can do and what we know how to get it to do. You can test it on a particular problem, and it fails. Then someone comes up with a different prompt, gives it a few examples, and suddenly it succeeds. So the failure doesn't necessarily establish a limit of the system. It may establish a limit of our ability to interact with it.

That means our evaluations give us something like a lower bound on its capabilities. We know it can do at least these things, under these conditions. But we don't have a complete inventory of everything it could do under every possible prompt or with access to different tools.

And from a safety perspective, that's a significant problem. We'd like to understand the capabilities before deployment. Instead, we're often discovering them afterward, as millions of people try different things.

r001.rationale: The response says a failure on one test may reflect an inability to interact with GPT-4 effectively and does not necessarily establish a limit of the system.

r002.rationale: The response describes capabilities that may emerge with different prompts or tools, but does not state that GPT-4 can have capabilities that were not explicitly designed into it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between what the system can do and what we know how to get it to do. Those are very different things. With GPT-4, we can test particular capabilities, but a failed test doesn’t necessarily establish a limit. Maybe a different prompt, a different set of tools, or more time would produce a successful result.

So we’re discovering capabilities through interaction rather than working from a complete understanding of the system. And that creates a problem for safety: if you don’t know the full range of capabilities, it’s difficult to make confident claims about what the system cannot do. Passing a collection of safety tests is evidence about those tests. It isn’t a guarantee about every situation the system might encounter.

r001.rationale: It says a failed test does not necessarily establish a limit, since another prompt, tools, or more time could reveal success.

r002.rationale: It describes unknown or undiscovered capabilities, but does not state that GPT-4 may have capabilities that were not explicitly designed into it.
